title: Kummerspeck — "grief bacon"
example_gloss: literally "grief bacon" — the weight you gain from emotional overeating
bridge_note: German just... has a word for this. One compound noun, no explanation needed if you're German.

title: A face that begs to be slapped
example_gloss: literally "a face in need of a slap"
bridge_note: Compound nouns let German build extremely specific insults in a single word — no phrase required.

title: "Girl" is grammatically neither male nor female
example_gloss: the girl (grammatically neuter, das — not feminine, die)
bridge_note: The diminutive suffix -chen always forces neuter gender, no matter what it's attached to. It overrides the natural gender of the word entirely — grammar wins over meaning.

title: A word that exists just to contradict "no"
example_gloss: You don't have time? — Yes I do! (doch specifically answers a negative question with a positive)
bridge_note: English has to add a whole extra word ("yes I do") to override a negative question. German just has a dedicated single-word rebuttal.

title: Compound nouns can run absurdly long
example_gloss: "law on the delegation of duties for the supervision of cattle marking and beef labeling" — a real, formerly official law name
bridge_note: German lets you glue nouns together indefinitely to build one exact-fit word instead of a phrase. There's no hard grammatical limit — just a limit on human patience.

title: The word English had to borrow whole
example_gloss: literally "harm-joy" — pleasure taken in someone else's misfortune
bridge_note: English speaks this word in German because English never bothered to compress the concept into one word of its own.
